triad.note: No source read uses the word 'triad' for duct + islet + vessel (the only 'triad' hits are clinical: Whipple, Virchow, etc.). Closest wording: larger islets lie along main/interlobular ducts; islet capillaries drain into the adjacent acinar capillary bed (insulo-acinar portal system). Say 'islets sit next to ducts and are richly vascularised', not 'triad'. The sources do not describe a terminal (intercalated) duct specifically paired with an islet; the duct association is stated for interlobular and main ducts, while small islets lie within lobules.

facts.fact: Larger islets are sited along the main and interlobular ducts; smaller islets are scattered through the acinar lobules
facts.value: most larger islets along main + interlobular ducts; small islets dispersed in lobules
facts.source: Beger 2023 ch.2 (Longnecker & Thompson) p19; Gorelick & Williams 2021 ch.1 (Longnecker) p11
facts.snippet: most larger islets lie along the main and interlobular ducts of the pancreas

facts.fact: Islet shape is often moulded by an adjacent duct
facts.value: irregular islets often reflect an adjacent structure, often a duct
facts.snippet: sometimes reflecting the presence of an adjacent structure, often a duct

facts.fact: Isolated islet cells also occur in association with ducts
facts.value: islet cells dispersed in lobules or ductal association
facts.snippet: isolated islet cells may be found dispersed in the acinar lobules or in association with ducts

facts.fact: Islet capillaries connect to the capillaries of neighbouring acini; the acinar cells next to an islet form a halo and get high islet-hormone exposure ('insulo-acinar portal system')
facts.value: insulo-acinar portal system (islet -> adjacent acinar capillary bed)
facts.snippet: has been referred to as an insulo-acinar portal system

facts.fact: Normal-tissue micrograph shows a small islet in a lobule beside a small intralobular duct/ductule, with a small artery and vein nearby (single image, not a stated rule)
facts.value: co-occurrence in one H&E field only
facts.source: Beger 2023 ch.2 (Longnecker & Thompson) Fig 2.10 caption p16; Gorelick & Williams 2021 ch.1 (Longnecker) Fig 27 caption p12
facts.snippet: A small vein (d) and artery (e) are at image right above center. A small islet is near the lower image right corner.

facts.fact: PanNET histology: tumour cells keep their orientation to the vasculature, like giant islets (supports islets being tightly vascular; not a duct-vessel-islet unit)
facts.snippet: preservation of the regular cords of monotonous cells and their orientation to the vasculature

facts.fact: Duct hierarchy: acinar tubules -> ductules (intercalated) -> small intralobular ducts -> interlobular ducts -> main duct (Wirsung) -> papilla; accessory duct of Santorini drains at the minor papilla in some people
facts.source: Beger 2023 ch.2 (Longnecker & Thompson) p17; Gorelick & Williams 2021 ch.1 (Longnecker) p7
facts.snippet: ductules that join to form the intralobular ducts, then into the interlobular ducts and main duct

facts.fact: Intralobular ducts are also called intercalated ductules and link acinar tubules to interlobular ducts
facts.snippet: intralobular ducts (sometimes called intercalated duct-ules) that link acinar tubules to the interlobular ducts

facts.fact: Interlobular ducts are the major branches draining into the main duct throughout the gland; they have thick collagenous walls with myofibroblasts and some smooth muscle, thinner than the main duct
facts.value: interlobular duct wall: collagenous, thinner than main
facts.source: Beger 2023 ch.2 (Longnecker & Thompson) p17; Gorelick & Williams 2021 ch.1 (Longnecker) Fig 26 p11
facts.snippet: The collagenous wall is conspicuous but clearly thinner than that of the main duct.

facts.fact: Smallest intralobular ducts and ductules have little or no connective-tissue wall and no smooth muscle; walls thicken progressively as ducts join
facts.value: wall thickness increases toward main duct
facts.snippet: The smallest intralobular ducts lack smooth muscle cells.

facts.fact: Duct lining is a single layer of cuboidal cells; centroacinar cells sit at the junction of acinus and ductule (may also lie within an acinar tubule)
facts.value: simple cuboidal; centroacinar at acinus-ductule junction
facts.source: Beger 2023 ch.2 (Longnecker & Thompson) p17; Gorelick & Williams 2021 ch.1 (Longnecker) Fig 15 p6
facts.snippet: Centroacinar cells (CACs) are typically located at the junction of an acinus or acinar tubule with a small ductule

facts.fact: Exocrine tissue is better described as an anastomosing tubular network that ends in some places as classic acini, not grape-like clusters on a branching duct
facts.value: acinar tubule network, not strict grapes
facts.source: Gorelick & Williams 2021 ch.1 (Longnecker) Fig 15 caption p6
facts.snippet: not arranged in clusters like grapes at the ends of a branching duct system but rather as an anastomosing tubular network

facts.fact: Interstitium around acinar lobules holds capillaries, arteries, veins, lymphatics, nerves, fat and stellate cells; acinar basal surface faces the interstitial space with vessels and nerves
facts.value: vessels/nerves in interstitium between acinar units
facts.source: Beger 2023 ch.2 (Longnecker & Thompson) p18 and Fig 2.11 caption p16
facts.snippet: The basal portion (B) of the acinar cells lies next to the interstitial space that contains vessels (V), nerves, and connective tissue.

facts.fact: Lobules are separated by connective-tissue septa (mesenchyme-derived); exocrine tissue is about 95%+ of mass, islets 1-2%
facts.source: Beger 2023 ch.2 p9 and early development chapter; Beger 2023 ch.2 (Longnecker & Thompson) p9
facts.snippet: The islets comprise 1–2% of pancreatic mass.
facts.confidence: medium (septa wording from developmental chapter: 'embryonic mesenchyme, which forms the septa that separate the many lobules')

facts.fact: Islet size 50-250 um (~70%), mean 100-150 um; ~0.5-1 million islets in adult human; possibly higher islet density in tail
facts.snippet: ~70% are in the size range 50–250 μm in diameter in humans, with an average in the range 100–150 μm

facts.fact: Islet cell mix in dorsal-anlage regions: beta 75-80%, alpha ~15%, delta ~5%, few PP; uncinate/ventral region is PP-rich with few alpha cells
facts.snippet: the majority of islet cells are β cells (75–80%), followed by α cells (about 15%)

facts.fact: Gross layout: head sits in the duodenal C-loop; neck lies anterior to the SMV/portal vein; body behind the stomach; tail near splenic hilum; no landmark between body and tail
facts.snippet: The tail of the pancreas lies near the hilum of the spleen.

facts.fact: PDAC is highly infiltrative: perineural and intravascular invasion present in practically all cases; nerves serve as pathways for spread beyond the pancreas
facts.snippet: Perineural and intravascular invasion are present in practically all cases

facts.fact: Vascular invasion leads to widespread dissemination, particularly to the liver; tumour cells may also creep along vessel endothelium or inside pre-existing ducts
facts.value: liver is the principal distant site
facts.snippet: Vascular invasion often leads to widespread dissemination of the neoplastic cells to other organs, particularly the liver.

facts.fact: Local spread: grows along nerves, invades blood vessels and retroperitoneum; can directly invade spleen, adrenals, transverse colon, stomach
facts.snippet: Pancreatic cancers often grow along nerves and invade into blood vessels and the retroperitoneum.

facts.fact: Nodal spread: peripancreatic, gastric, mesenteric, omental and portohepatic nodes often involved; distant mets principally liver and lungs
facts.snippet: Distant metastases occur, principally to the liver and lungs.

facts.fact: Most patients present with locally advanced disease (vascular involvement) or widespread metastasis, generally to liver and peritoneum; <20% resectable
facts.value: liver + peritoneum are the usual metastatic sites
facts.source: Kleeff 2016 Nat Rev Dis Primers p10
facts.snippet: widespread metastatic disease, generally to the liver and peritoneum

facts.fact: Stage at diagnosis: ~10-20% resectable, 30-40% borderline/locally advanced, 50-60% metastatic (Kleeff); 15-20% resectable, 40-50% metastatic, 30-40% locally advanced (Beger ch.134)
facts.source: Kleeff 2016 p(Surgery section); Beger 2023 ch.134 (Lindberg et al.) p1037
facts.snippet: harbor metastatic disease (40–50%) or locally advanced tumors (30–40%)

facts.fact: Over 80% of patients have unresectable disease at diagnosis from local invasion and/or distant liver and peritoneal metastases; occult peritoneal and small surface liver mets often missed on imaging
facts.snippet: distant metastases involving the liver and peritoneum

facts.fact: Body/tail tumours carry higher risk of peritoneal dissemination than head tumours because they face the free lesser sac
facts.snippet: Body and tail tumors are at higher risk of peritoneal dissemination than head tumors

facts.fact: Occult sites at laparoscopy: posterior liver surface, paraduodenal retroperitoneum, proximal jejunal mesentery, lesser sac; Douglas pouch for cytology
facts.snippet: posterior liver surface, paraduodenal retroperitoneum, proximal jejunal mesentery, and lesser sac are possible sites

facts.fact: Clinical nodal/peritoneal markers: Virchow node (supraclavicular), Sister Mary Joseph node (umbilical), Blumer shelf (pelvic peritoneal implants)
facts.snippet: Involved supraclavicular (Virchow’s node) or umbilical (Sister Mary Joseph node) nodes

facts.fact: After resection ~76% recur (877-patient series); liver-only or multi-site recurrence has worse survival than lung-only or local-only recurrence; isolated lung metastases are rare
facts.source: Beger 2023 ch.155 (recurrence) p1213, citing Groot et al.
facts.snippet: Six-hundred sixty-two (76%) of the 877 patients had disease recurrence

facts.fact: Per-organ percentages (liver x%, lung y%, peritoneum z%) are NOT given in the sources read; only ordering (liver first, then peritoneum and lung, plus nodes)
facts.snippet: (none)

tumour_locations.frequency: Commonest; 75-80% of resected pancreatic neoplasms at Johns Hopkins (Kleeff Fig 1). The 85-90% figure was not found in the sources read.
tumour_locations.source: Robbins 9e ch.19 p893-894; Beger 2023 ch.125 p958; Kleeff 2016 Fig 1

tumour_locations.location: Anywhere along the gland (no head/tail predilection stated), or in peripancreatic tissue
tumour_locations.frequency: ~2% of pancreatic neoplasms (Robbins) / <3% (Beger ch.98); 15-20% of resected neoplasms in a surgical series (Kleeff Fig 1); 7% of resected cystic neoplasms
tumour_locations.source: Robbins 9e ch.24 p1121; Beger 2023 ch.98 p753; Kleeff 2016 Fig 1; Beger ch.80 p620

tumour_locations.location: Location not stated in sources read (bulky, well-circumscribed, fleshy mass)
